content.text:
Wrote `verbdata/gloss-review/shards/gloss_039.out.json`. Three findings out of 51 verbs (~6%, in line with the expected rate):

- **`verschlagen`** (high) — "drive, strand, shlep, bring" is an unfiltered synonym pile; *shlep* is opaque to a learner and *bring* names nothing. → `strand, drive somewhere`
- **`versehen`** (high) — "equip, make mistake" fuses the transitive sense (candidate 3) with the reflexive *sich versehen* (candidate 4) into one comma list, so the house style reads two unrelated senses as synonyms. → `provide with, furnish`
- **`verstoßen`** (low) — "violate, expel" pairs *gegen etwas verstoßen* with *jemanden verstoßen*; the rule-breaking sense is the frequent one. → `violate, infringe`

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- This shard is nearly all `ver-` inseparables, and that prefix is unusually productive in exactly the way that breaks dictionaries: it can mean *away* (`verschenken`), *wrongly* (`sich versehen`, `sich versprechen`), *completely/up* (`verschlingen`), or *cause-to-be* (`verstärken`). kaikki lists all four readings flatly, so the two high-severity defects here are both **cross-reading comma lists** — a shortener collapsed a *wrongly*-sense and an ordinary-sense into one line.
- That suggests a mechanical screen worth running across the whole corpus: any `ver-` verb whose gloss contains both a neutral action verb and an error/mistake word is a strong candidate for the same defect.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`
